sharedRules.audience: Curious beginners with no assumed knowledge of Japan. Terms are introduced before testing them.
sharedRules.flow: Four interleaved content sections and five topic questions, then scheduled earlier-lesson review, then completion.
sharedRules.narration: Hidden narrator; Mepamo-kun acts silently. Narration text doubles as the on-screen transcript. Word highlighting and auto-transition apply only to narrated sections.
sharedRules.practice: No voice-over. Select/place -> Check -> explanation -> Continue. Never auto-advance practice or feedback.
sharedRules.sounds: Reuse Lesson 1 / existing project celebration for correct answers and a neutral sound for incorrect answers, respecting mute. No sounds were generated for these drafts.
sharedRules.branding: Existing repository tokens, logo, mascot and components are authoritative. Reference screenshots specify layout intent; never hardcode a second theme to match them.
sharedRules.pictureDescriptions: Author notes retained for context; artwork.path is the supplied file to render. All paths are relative to package root.
sharedRules.grading: Correct answers are author metadata. Do not expose answer IDs, checkmarks or the key before Check. Keep correctness separate from selected state.
sharedRules.timing: Aim for roughly one minute of narration per lesson at a comfortable pace. Counts below are script-based estimates, not recorded audio durations. Do not pad interactions to force a duration.
sharedRules.matching: A proposed question format. Reuse an existing matching component if available; do not assume it already exists in the repository.
sharedRules.sourceNote: Facts checked against primary government, tourism-authority, operator and UNESCO sources on 2026-11-06. Sources are author notes, not narrator speech.
sharedRules.imagesIncluded: 31 native-resolution crops extracted from approved mockups; no new pictures generated for this handoff.

lessons.title: Kyoto: A capital with a long memory
lessons.storyFocus: From imperial capital to living traditions.

modules.title: A capital with a long memory.
modules.narration: Tokyo is Japan’s capital today. But in 794, the imperial court—the emperor and the people around him—moved to a city called Heian-kyo, now Kyoto. The court remained there for over a thousand years, until the emperor moved to Tokyo in 1869.

artworks.alt: An illustrated historic court building and garden in Kyoto, with Mepamo-kun.

modules.title: Two kinds of sacred place.
modules.narration: Across Kyoto, sacred places tell different stories. Buddhist temples belong to Buddhism. Shinto shrines belong to Shinto, another religious tradition in Japan. A torii gate often marks a shrine entrance. These traditions have also influenced the city’s architecture and cultural life.

artworks.alt: A red torii gate in front of a Shinto shrine.

modules.visualNote: Use shrine image for the Shinto/torii explanation; it must not be labeled as a Buddhist temple. Keep the two definitions as live text.

modules.title: Culture in a bowl.
modules.narration: Tradition can be something you do. In a tea ceremony, a host carefully prepares and serves matcha—powdered green tea. The bowl, utensils, and attention given to guests turn serving tea into a cultural practice. Kyoto’s crafts help make that experience possible.

artworks.alt: A bowl of green matcha beside a bamboo whisk.

modules.title: Still being made.
modules.narration: Kyoto’s traditions continue beyond old buildings. Artisans weave textiles, dye fabric, and make pottery, passing skills to others while creating new designs. The city’s history lives through people who keep practicing and adapting it. An old capital can still make something new.

artworks.alt: A loom with patterned fabric and spools of thread.

lessons.title: Osaka: The story behind the flavor
lessons.storyFocus: How a commercial city’s trading networks connect with its food culture.

modules.title: Follow the ingredients.
modules.narration: Why is Osaka called “the nation’s kitchen”? During the Edo period, ships brought rice and other goods here from across Japan. Merchants stored, bought, and sold them. Osaka grew as a commercial city—a place where trade helped shape everyday life.

artworks.alt: A canal-side trading district with rice cargo and Mepamo-kun.

modules.title: Two familiar favorites.
modules.narration: That food story continues at the griddle. Takoyaki are small balls of batter with pieces of octopus inside. Osaka-style okonomiyaki is a savory pancake made with batter and cabbage, often with other ingredients. Both became well-known parts of the city’s food culture.

artworks.alt: Round takoyaki balls, one cut open to show octopus inside.
A savory okonomiyaki pancake on a plate.

modules.title: The flavor underneath.
modules.narration: Look beneath the toppings and you may find dashi: a savory cooking stock. In Osaka, a familiar version combines kombu—edible kelp—with dried bonito fish flakes. Dashi gives depth to many dishes. It is a base flavor, rather than simply a sauce poured on top.
modules.visualNote: No dashi illustration is present in these mockups. Use existing project ingredient imagery only if accurate; otherwise present this short explanation in the existing text-focused module variant. Never label takoyaki or matcha as dashi.

modules.title: A city connected by food.
modules.narration: Trade and cooking belong to the same story. Ingredients arriving from different regions gave merchants something to sell and cooks something to work with. A useful way to follow this connection is: ingredients arrive, markets distribute them, and cooks turn them into dishes.

artworks.alt: A cargo ship carrying ingredients from other regions.
A cook turns ingredients into a dish in a pan.

lessons.title: Mount Fuji: More than a mountain
lessons.storyFocus: How a natural mountain can be recognized for its cultural meaning.

modules.title: A mountain you may recognize.
modules.narration: A broad base, sloping sides, and a summit often capped with snow: this is Mount Fuji, also called Fujisan. At 3,776 meters, it is Japan’s highest mountain. It is also a volcano. Its importance, though, reaches far beyond its height.

artworks.alt: Mount Fuji above a lake, with Mepamo-kun in the foreground.

modules.title: A journey with meaning.
modules.narration: For centuries, people have approached Fuji as a sacred place. Pilgrims made journeys connected to religious belief, including ascents of the mountain and visits to shrines around its base. A pilgrimage is a journey with religious meaning, not simply another word for sightseeing.

artworks.alt: A shrine associated with Mount Fuji, with Mepamo-kun nearby.

modules.title: A mountain on paper.
modules.narration: Others encountered Fuji through art. The artist Katsushika Hokusai made it a recurring subject in his woodblock-print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. A woodblock print transfers an image from a carved block onto paper. These images helped carry Fuji’s silhouette to audiences far away.

artworks.alt: A woodblock-style illustration of waves and Mount Fuji.

modules.title: Why cultural heritage?
modules.narration: In 2013, UNESCO added Fujisan to the World Heritage List as a cultural site. The recognition centers on its sacred associations and artistic inspiration. The property includes places around the mountain as well as parts of Fuji itself. Nature can hold meaning created through human culture.

artworks.alt: A pilgrim at a shrine and a picture of Mount Fuji.

lessons.title: Shinkansen: Connecting the cities
lessons.storyFocus: From a recognizable train to the railway system and city connections behind it.

modules.title: A new way between cities.
modules.narration: A streamlined train leaves the station. It belongs to the Shinkansen, Japan’s high-speed railway network, often called the bullet train. The first line, the Tokaido Shinkansen, opened in 1964, linking Tokyo and Shin-Osaka. Other lines later extended high-speed rail to more regions.

artworks.alt: A Shinkansen train on elevated tracks, with Mepamo-kun.

modules.title: Put the cities together.
modules.narration: Follow the Tokaido route from Tokyo toward Osaka. Among its major stations, you encounter Nagoya, then Kyoto, then Shin-Osaka. Shin-Osaka is the Shinkansen station serving Osaka; it is different from Osaka Station. This simplified sequence leaves out other stations along the line.
modules.visualNote: Render Tokyo → Nagoya → Kyoto → Shin-Osaka as live station labels using existing tokens; this is a simplified sequence, not a geographic map or every stop.

modules.title: More than a fast train.
modules.narration: The Tokaido Shinkansen works as a system. Passenger trains carry people; dedicated tracks provide their route; automatic train control helps regulate speed. Its high-speed tracks have no road level crossings. Carefully designed infrastructure matters as much as the train’s streamlined appearance.

artworks.alt: Dedicated railway tracks beneath overhead power lines.

modules.title: What speed connects.
modules.narration: The important change is what faster connections make possible: people can travel between major cities for work, visits, and time with family. The Shinkansen links those cities; local transport serves different needs within them. Its story is about connections, as well as speed.

artworks.alt: Tokyo and Kyoto connected by a high-speed train.
